Equipment showing ethanol being heated under reflux

specPoints.text: know that ethanol can be oxidised by: burning in air or oxygen (complete combustion); reaction with oxygen in the air to form ethanoic acid (microbial oxidation); heating with potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid to form ethanoic acid

primer.text: From Alcohols you already know ethanol as the two-carbon member of the organic family, with its reactive -OH group sitting at the end of the chain. This note tracks what happens when that molecule meets oxygen: three separate routes that all carry ethanol towards the same acid.

lessons.title: Three routes that oxidise ethanol
lessons.opening: Ethanol does not survive contact with oxygen untouched. This lesson walks the three routes that oxidise it: burning it as a fuel, letting airborne bacteria sour it, and handing it to a chemical oxidising agent. Each route ends at a different product, and telling them apart is exactly what the exam asks.
keyPoints: Alcohols burn in air to form carbon dioxide and water.
Ethanol burns with an almost invisible blue flame, so laboratories use it in spirit burners.
Airborne acetobacter bacteria use oxygen to turn the ethanol in open wine into ethanoic acid.
Wine left open for days tastes acidic and vinegary because microbial action makes ethanoic acid.
The microbial route is the same chemistry that produces the acid used in vinegar.

low.restatement: Ethanol can be changed by oxygen in three ways. Burning gives carbon dioxide and water. Bacteria in the air also attack open wine and leave sour ethanoic acid behind.
low.analogy: Think of ethanol as a loaf of bread and airborne bacteria as mould spores: one route burns the loaf up at once, the other slowly spoils it, and both change it for good.
low.examPointer: Learn all three oxidation routes as a list; questions ask you to name the product or the agent for a named route.

medium.restatement: Complete burning turns ethanol into carbon dioxide and water with a pale, almost invisible flame. Airborne acetobacter bacteria instead convert exposed ethanol into a weak ethanoic acid mixture, which is why abandoned wine tastes vinegary.
medium.analogy: One molecule, two easy doors: the fire door burns ethanol straight to carbon dioxide and water, while the airy door lets bacteria sour it towards vinegar over several days.
medium.examPointer: Only the burning route produces carbon dioxide; both microbial action and dichromate treatment deliver ethanoic acid instead.

check.stem: Ethanol burns completely in air. Which products form?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water
options.explanation: Complete burning of any alcohol delivers exactly these two products.

options.text: Ethanoic acid and water
options.explanation: That pair belongs to the microbial and dichromate routes, not to burning.
options.misconception: all routes share one product set

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water
options.explanation: Carbon monoxide only appears when the oxygen supply is limited and burning is incomplete.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen
options.explanation: Hydrogen is never released by burning an alcohol; the hydrogen ends up in water.

check.stem: Why do school laboratories choose ethanol for spirit burners?

options.text: It burns cleanly, with little smell and a flame that is hard to see
options.explanation: The clean burn and faint blue flame make it practical for classroom heating.

options.text: It is the only alcohol that can burn at all
options.explanation: All alcohols burn; ethanol is chosen for the character of its flame, not exclusivity.

options.text: It evaporates too slowly to catch fire accidentally
options.explanation: Ethanol is actually quite volatile; safety comes from its clean, odour-free burn.

options.text: It produces a bright yellow flame that is easy to see
options.explanation: The opposite is true: the flame is almost invisible and pale blue.

check.stem: Wine left open for several days tastes vinegary. Which process caused this?

options.text: Airborne bacteria oxidising the ethanol
options.explanation: Acetobacter uses oxygen from the air to convert ethanol into ethanoic acid.

options.text: Complete combustion inside the bottle
options.explanation: No flame or ample oxygen exists in a bottle; burning cannot happen there.

options.text: Heating with potassium dichromate(VI)
options.explanation: That is the laboratory method and nothing in an opened wine bottle supplies it.

options.text: Water evaporating and concentrating the flavour
options.explanation: The sourness comes from a new acid being made, not from existing flavours concentrating.

check.stem: Which acid forms when oxygen in the air oxidises ethanol?

options.text: Ethanoic acid
options.explanation: The two-carbon alcohol keeps its two carbons and gains the carboxylic acid group.

options.text: Methanoic acid
options.explanation: Methanoic acid has only one carbon; ethanol has two and does not lose one.

options.text: Propanoic acid
options.explanation: Propanoic acid carries three carbons, one more than ethanol can offer.

options.text: Ethanedioic acid
options.explanation: The two-carbon product here carries one -COOH group, not one at each end.

check.stem: Which word equation describes the microbial route?

options.text: ethanol + oxygen makes ethanoic acid + water
options.explanation: Bacterial action adds one oxygen atom to ethanol and leaves water as the second product.

options.text: ethanol + oxygen makes carbon dioxide + water
options.explanation: That is the complete combustion equation, a different route with different products.

options.text: ethanol makes ethanoic acid with nothing else formed
options.explanation: Water is always the second product of this route; mass has to balance.

options.text: ethanol + water makes ethanoic acid + oxygen
options.explanation: The route consumes oxygen; it does not produce it, and water is not an input.

lessons.title: Oxidising agents and the reflux method
lessons.opening: The laboratory route to ethanoic acid heats ethanol under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). The equation hides the oxidiser behind the bracket symbol [O], and the flask itself tells the story as orange drains to green. This lesson unpacks the equation, the apparatus and the colour change.
keyPoints: Heating ethanol with potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid produces ethanoic acid.
The equation is written CH3CH2OH + [O] giving CH3COOH + H2O.
The symbol [O] stands for oxygen supplied by the oxidising agent.
A condenser above the flask stops volatile liquids escaping during the hour-long boil.
The dichromate mixture turns from orange to green as the reaction proceeds.

low.restatement: Heating ethanol with potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid makes ethanoic acid. The bracket [O] stands for the oxygen delivered, and the mixture changes from orange to green.
low.analogy: The dichromate behaves like a courier carrying oxygen atoms: it drops one off at the ethanol and fades from orange to green as payment for the delivery.
low.examPointer: Quote the colour change from orange to green; it is the classic observation mark for this reaction.

medium.restatement: Refluxing ethanol with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) converts CH3CH2OH into CH3COOH, with [O] standing for the oxygen supplied. A condenser returns escaping vapours so the long boil loses no volatile liquid, and the orange mixture ends up green.
medium.analogy: A condenser above the flask works like a lid that drips escaping steam back into the pot: everything volatile returns, so only the chemistry changes while the ingredients stay.
medium.examPointer: When balancing the burning equation, remember ethanol already carries an oxygen atom of its own; forgetting it is the named examiner trap.

check.stem: Which reagent mixture oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid in the laboratory?

options.text: Potassium dichromate(VI) heated in dilute sulfuric acid
options.explanation: Acidified dichromate is the standard laboratory oxidising mixture for this change.

options.text: Potassium carbonate dissolved in water
options.explanation: A carbonate solution is mildly alkaline and cannot oxidise the alcohol.

options.text: Concentrated sodium chloride solution
options.explanation: Salt water contains no oxidising agent capable of attacking ethanol.

options.text: Magnesium ribbon in dilute sulfuric acid
options.explanation: That mixture makes hydrogen; it does not oxidise ethanol.

check.stem: What does [O] represent in the equation CH3CH2OH + [O] gives CH3COOH + H2O?

options.text: Oxygen supplied by the oxidising agent
options.explanation: Square brackets are shorthand for oxygen delivered by the dichromate.

options.text: One molecule of oxygen gas, O2
options.explanation: The bracket notation counts single oxygen atoms, not O2 molecules.

options.text: An oxygen ion carrying a charge
options.explanation: No ionic charge is implied; the notation just bookkeeps the oxygen added.

options.text: Ozone acting as the oxidiser
options.explanation: Ozone plays no part here; dichromate is the named oxidising agent.

check.stem: Which colour change shows the dichromate reaction has occurred?

options.text: Orange to green
options.explanation: The dichromate is orange at first and green once it has delivered its oxygen.

options.text: Green to orange
options.explanation: The direction is reversed; the starting mixture is the orange one.

options.text: Blue to colourless
options.explanation: That description belongs to other tests, not to acidified dichromate.

options.text: Colourless to pink
options.explanation: No indicator is present; the colour story belongs to the dichromate itself.

check.stem: Why is a condenser placed above the reaction flask?

options.text: It returns escaping vapours so volatile liquids are not lost during the long boil
options.explanation: The mixture boils for about an hour, and the condenser keeps every volatile ingredient inside.

options.text: It raises the pressure so the reaction goes faster
options.explanation: A condenser does not pressurise the flask; its job is condensing vapour.

options.text: It filters the green chromium compounds out of the mixture
options.explanation: Nothing is filtered; the green colour simply stays in the flask.

options.text: It feeds oxygen from the air into the reaction
options.explanation: The oxygen comes from the dichromate, not from air drawn through the condenser.

check.stem: Students often balance the combustion equation of ethanol incorrectly. What must they remember?

options.text: The ethanol molecule already contains an oxygen atom
options.explanation: That oxygen contributes to the products, so the oxygen count cannot be balanced from O2 alone.

options.text: Ethanol contains no oxygen, so extra gas is never needed
options.explanation: The -OH group means ethanol does carry oxygen and burning still needs O2.

options.text: Water is not one of the products
options.explanation: Water is always a product when an alcohol burns completely.

options.text: The number of carbon atoms changes during burning
options.explanation: Atoms are conserved; every carbon in ethanol ends up in carbon dioxide.

glossary.definition: A change that adds oxygen or removes hydrogen from a substance; ethanol undergoes it by burning, by microbial action or by dichromate treatment.
Burning a fuel in plenty of oxygen so that the only products are carbon dioxide and water.
The carboxylic acid CH3COOH made when ethanol is oxidised; it is the acid that gives vinegar its sour taste.
Heating a boiling mixture beneath a condenser so that volatile liquids return to the flask instead of escaping.
Potassium dichromate(VI), the orange oxidising agent that turns green as it delivers oxygen to ethanol in dilute sulfuric acid.

workedExample.prompt: State the product and conditions for each oxidation route of ethanol: a) complete combustion; b) microbial oxidation; c) heating with an oxidising agent. d) What observation shows the dichromate reaction has occurred?
steps: a) Burning in air (complete combustion) gives carbon dioxide and water.
b) Microbial oxidation: airborne acetobacter bacteria use oxygen in the air to convert exposed ethanol into ethanoic acid — the vinegary taste of wine left open for several days.
c) Heating under reflux with potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid gives ethanoic acid: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3COOH + H2O, where [O] represents the oxygen supplied by the oxidising agent.
d) The potassium dichromate turns from orange to green as the reaction proceeds.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) CO2 and H2O. b) Ethanoic acid (air oxygen + bacteria). c) Ethanoic acid; CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3COOH + H2O. d) Orange turns to green.
